enrichment.short_title: Finance company entitled to reject trucks sold by invoice without fitted bodies
key_facts: Iveco Finance paid Man Truck over £474,000 for six refrigerated trucks after receiving invoices describing complete trucks with Gray & Adams fridge bodies fitted.
The chassis had been delivered to Gray & Adams for bodywork but the bodies had not been fitted when Iveco paid and leased the vehicles to City Truck Group, which later entered administration.
Man contended it had no contract with Iveco and, if it did, had only contracted to supply chassis to City's order rather than complete trucks.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Gray J's summary judgment for Iveco for over £1 million.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; summary judgment upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a supplier invoices a finance company for trucks 'supplied and fitted' with specified equipment and the finance company pays, an objective analysis shows a contract of sale by description between supplier and finance company; rejection is available where goods do not correspond with that description, and neither a prior arrangement with the end customer nor alleged agency displaces the contract formed by invoice and payment.

Whether an earlier contract between Man and City displaced the finance-company sale
Whether Man was in breach where chassis were supplied but fridge bodies were not fitted

enrichment.short_title: Hospital doctor not liable for failing to re-warn of chickenpox fetal risk
key_facts: Dr Curtis, a locum GP, negligently failed to warn Miss Wyatt about risks to her unborn child from chickenpox at 13–14 weeks; causation against her was established at trial.
Four and a half weeks later, at an antenatal appointment, Dr Howarth discussed chickenpox but did not expressly warn of serious fetal abnormality risks; the child was born with serious abnormalities.
Dr Curtis brought Part 20 proceedings against the hospital authority for contribution; the trial judge dismissed them on liability and causation grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by Dr Curtis against dismissal of her Part 20 contribution claim; permission to appeal against primary liability finding had already been refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Dr Howarth held not negligent and permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: On the facts found, a hospital doctor who gently raised chickenpox in antenatal consultation and was reassured that advice had already been given by another doctor was not negligent for failing to probe or re-state fetal abnormality risks; under Sidaway the Bolam threshold applied where the patient had not solicited advice, and the judge's flawed causation reasoning did not assist Dr Curtis once liability failed.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Howarth breached his duty of care in antenatal consultation
Whether Sidaway or Pearce governed the duty to volunteer risk information
Whether failure to warn Dr Howarth's negligence caused Miss Wyatt not to terminate at 18 weeks
Whether a second doctor must investigate prior advice given by another doctor

enrichment.short_title: Anglesey housing benefit subsidy recovery upheld under Paragraph 6

statutes_considered.name: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Anglesey paid about £2.2 million housing benefit on renewed claims without fresh Rent Officer determinations and received subsidy it was not entitled to.
The Secretary of State exercised discretion under section 140C(3) to recover only 20% (£444,661) using a percentage banding policy after earlier Bridgnorth/West Oxfordshire litigation.
Anglesey challenged both the lawfulness of Schedule 4 paragraph 6 (nil subsidy where renewal referrals omitted) and the reasonableness of the recovery decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision to recover overpaid housing benefit subsidy; permission to appeal granted on compelling reasons.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; paragraph 6 held lawful and the 20% recovery decision Wednesbury reasonable; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 6 of Schedule 4 to the 1998 Subsidy Order, providing nil subsidy where required Rent Officer referrals on renewal claims were omitted, is not an unlawful or disproportionate legislative sanction especially where section 140C(3) allows partial recovery; a banded percentage recovery reflecting systemic administrative failure can be a lawful exercise of discretion even where there was no net loss to the public purse.

Whether recovery of 20% subsidy was a lawful exercise of section 140C(3) discretion

enrichment.short_title: Compromise to discontinue void for common mistake on claim form service
key_facts: Miss Brennan alleged carbon monoxide exposure from a faulty boiler in an Islington Council flat over many years; multiple firms of solicitors handled her claim with severe delay.

After a Recorder held the claim form was not validly served within four months, the Council's solicitor and Miss Brennan's solicitor orally agreed to discontinue the claim against the Council on a no-costs basis.
The Court of Appeal later reversed McCombe J in Anderton v Clwyd, establishing valid service; Miss Brennan sought to set aside the compromise as based on a common mistake of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by Miss Brennan against Deputy Master Eastman's refusal to stay the Council action on the ground the compromise was void for common mistake of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; compromise held void ab initio for common fundamental mistake that the claim form had not been validly served.
enrichment.ratio: A compromise agreement may be void for common mistake of law where both parties shared the fundamental assumption that the claim form had not been validly served and the action was doomed; following Kleinwort Benson, the mistake-of-law bar should not survive in contract/compromise cases, and this was not a give-and-take settlement but a agreement whose only springboard was the mistaken legal assumption.

Whether the Unibank v Laib action remained extant after mortgagee sale satisfied the debt
Whether CSI International v Archway Personnel applied
Whether the settlement was a compromise of doubtful rights or agreement on a shared legal precondition

enrichment.short_title: Custody time limit extension quashed for inadequate listing inquiry
key_facts: Khan was charged with two counts of wounding with intent, remanded in custody from March 2003, with trial fixed for 5 August 2003.
On 4 August the listing office removed the fixture after unexpected trials occupied the court on the preceding Monday; custody time limits were due to expire on 5 September.
On 4 September HHJ McCahill extended custody time limits to 17 January 2004 without rigorous inquiry into why the competing case took priority or alternative listing options.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Wolverhampton Crown Court decision extending custody time limits under section 22(3).
enrichment.outcome: Extension decision quashed as Wednesbury unreasonable for failure to conduct sufficiently rigorous inquiry; bail conditions subsequently negotiated.
enrichment.ratio: Although court unavailability can be good and sufficient cause to extend custody time limits, a judge must rigorously examine why an earlier trial date could not be maintained and why competing cases prevailed; extending limits without adequate information about the case that displaced the fixture or realistic earlier listing alternatives is susceptible to judicial review.

Whether the Crown Court judge conducted a sufficiently rigorous inquiry

enrichment.short_title: Joint tortfeasor pleading struck out unless further particulars supplied
key_facts: Ablaise sued Nettec Plc and Nettec Solutions for patent infringement relating to interactive website services; Nettec Plc claimed to be non-trading since January 2001.

Direct infringement allegations were accepted as arguable, but paragraph 6 pleaded joint tortfeasance by common design in sparse terms relying on common directors, corporate presentation as Nettec Plc, consolidated accounts, and parent-subsidiary relationship.
Claimant refused to amend despite substantial evidence suggesting Nettec Plc involvement, insisting on deficient pleading supplemented by evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out joint tortfeasance allegation against first defendant in patent infringement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Paragraph 6 ordered struck out unless claimant provided full particulars of joint tortfeasance by 14 November; direct infringement claims to continue.
enrichment.ratio: Joint tortfeasance requires conspiracy, procurement or inducement and some taking part in furtherance of a common design, not mere common directorship, subsidiary status, or outward corporate presentation; sparse pleading cannot survive even where evidence might support an arguable case if the claimant refuses to particularise properly.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 6 adequately pleaded joint tortfeasance by common design
Whether common directors and parent-subsidiary relationship suffice for joint liability

enrichment.short_title: Mortgagee sale does not end action so solicitor negligence claim survives
key_facts: Mr Laib borrowed in Deutschmarks from Unibank secured on his London flat; Unibank obtained possession in 1996 while the money claim stood over with liberty to restore.
After solicitor Mr Kalim died, new solicitors agreed with the Council to discontinue the first action believing the claim form had not been validly served within four months.
The property was sold in November 1996 and the mortgage debt satisfied with a surplus to Mr Laib; Master Foster struck out the solicitor negligence claim applying CSI International.

enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; CSI International distinguished and negligence claim after 26 November 1996 held arguable.
enrichment.ratio: CSI International applies where a money judgment has been fully satisfied and no counterclaim was pleaded before satisfaction; where only a possession order has been enforced and the money claim remains extant with liberty to restore, satisfaction of the secured debt by mortgagee sale does not terminate the action, so a counterclaim against the mortgagee and related solicitor negligence claims are not barred by that principle.

enrichment.short_title: Patent claimant ordered to provide £320,000 security for costs
key_facts: Ablaise Ltd, an impecunious company, brought High Court patent infringement proceedings with a five-to-seven-day trial estimate; defendants estimated future costs from CMC to trial at about £490,000.
An earlier £60,000 security order had been paid; defendants now sought about £320,000 (two-thirds of future costs) for the post-CMC period.
Claimant failed to demonstrate litigation would be stifled: shareholders including Mark Bernstein had substantial undisclosed assets and incomplete financial disclosure undermined stifling argument.

enrichment.outcome: Security for costs ordered in the sum of £320,000 for period from CMC to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Under Keary Developments, a claimant must prove it is probable the claim would be stifled by an order for security, including showing inability to raise funds from directors, shareholders or backers; incomplete disclosure of shareholder resources and neutral prospects of success do not justify refusing security where defendants face certain irrecoverable costs if successful.

enrichment.short_title: No negligence in M62 safety fence length after Selby rail crash
key_facts: On 28 February 2001 Hart fell asleep driving on the M62; his Land Rover and trailer left the carriageway, descended an embankment and fouled the East Coast Main Line, causing a derailment in which ten people died.
Hart's insurers, by subrogation, sought contribution from the Secretary of State for Transport alleging the approach safety fence at Little Heck Bridge was negligently too short by about 7 metres.
Expert evidence showed the 33.5-metre full-height fence met TD 19/85 and BE5 minimum standards and post-accident risk ranking scored the site as low risk.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of contribution claim under the 1978 Act following Hart's admitted liability in Selby disaster litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Contribution claim dismissed; Department of Transport not negligent in 1974 design or 1993/1995 maintenance of safety fence.
enrichment.ratio: A highway authority owes a duty to take reasonable care to users of the highway and foreseeable victims on neighbouring land when creating bridge approaches over railways, but the length of approach safety fencing is a site-specific exercise of professional judgment judged by Bolam; meeting long-standing minimum standards and low ex post risk assessment can defeat negligence even where a longer fence might have prevented a particular incursion.
legal_issues: Whether the Department owed a duty of care to persons on the railway line
Whether the approach safety fence length was negligently short in 1974
Whether Bolam or hindsight negligence standard applied to fence design
Whether 1993/1995 reconstruction created fresh negligence
Whether ex turpi causa barred Hart's contribution claim

statutes_considered.name: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Four Avon-area unitary authorities jointly adopted a replacement structure plan including Policy 37 on Gypsy and traveller site provision.
The examination panel recommended that local plans 'identify suitable locations' for Gypsy sites, reflecting failure of existing criteria-only policies.

enrichment.ratio: Where an examination panel recommends that local plans identify suitable Gypsy site locations rather than merely set criteria, adopting a structure plan policy that only requires criteria-based local plan policies is a departure from the recommendation triggering regulation 15(4); authorities may depart but must list non-accepted recommendations and invite objections before adoption.
